title: Accounting Changes & Error Corrections
description: Understand changes in accounting principles, estimates and corrections of prior-period errors.
html:
Not every accounting change is treated the same

A major exam skill is identifying exactly what type of change occurred.

Main categories

  • Change in accounting principle
  • Change in accounting estimate
  • Change in reporting entity
  • Correction of an error

Change in accounting principle

This occurs when a company changes from one generally accepted accounting principle to another generally accepted accounting principle.

When required and practicable, a change in accounting principle is generally applied retrospectively.

Retrospective application

Prior-period financial statements presented are generally adjusted as though the new principle had been used in those periods, subject to the applicable guidance and practicability rules.

Change in accounting estimate

Estimates change because new information or experience becomes available.

Changes in estimates are generally accounted for prospectively.

Example

Equipment originally had an estimated useful life of 10 years.

Based on new information, management changes its estimate of the remaining useful life.

Prior financial statements are generally not rewritten simply because the estimate changed.

The new estimate affects the current and future periods as applicable.

Change in reporting entity

A change in reporting entity generally requires retrospective application to financial statements of prior periods presented.

Error correction

An error is different from a legitimate change in estimate.

Examples can include mathematical mistakes, incorrect application of accounting principles, or oversight or misuse of facts that existed when the financial statements were prepared.

Prior-period errors

Material errors in previously issued financial statements generally require correction through restatement of prior-period financial statements when presented, along with the appropriate beginning-equity adjustment when necessary.

Comparison

Principle

Generally retrospective

Estimate

Prospective

Reporting Entity

Generally retrospective

Error

Prior-period correction / restatement

Important warning

Some situations have special guidance. Do not assume that every change involving an accounting method automatically follows the same treatment.

quiz.prompt: A company revises the estimated remaining useful life of equipment because of new information. How is the change generally accounted for?

choices.text: Retrospectively by rewriting all prior years
Prospectively in the current and future periods affected

quiz.explanation: A revision based on new information is generally a change in accounting estimate and is accounted for prospectively.

objectives: Explain accounting changes & error corrections and its underlying principles.
